details:
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive prototype for exploring surface change over time. Users can switch among four study areas—Jakobshavn Glacier, Thwaites Glacier, Kīlauea Volcano, and the San Andreas Fault—and scrub or play through quarterly dates from 2022 to 2025. The map, summary metrics, and history chart update with the selected date. Users can change map layers and light/dark themes, inspect sample points, and export observations as CSV.

The map uses real, date-matched MODIS Terra Corrected Reflectance True Color imagery from NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) for geographic context. NASA GIBS documentation The displacement values, vectors, and metrics are simulated. MODIS is optical imagery, not SAR, and it does not generate or validate the motion results.

The project makes remote-sensing ideas easier to explore by combining satellite imagery with an interactive timeline. Its intended impact is to help students and the public understand how Earth-observation tools can reveal change, and to create a foundation for integrating validated SAR displacement products in future versions.

We built the application in Python. FastAPI and Uvicorn provide the local API; Flask serves the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript interface. PyDeck and Deck.gl render the map, while PyWebView displays the app in a Windows desktop window and PyInstaller packages it as an executable. No specialized hardware is required.

The creative element is making the map and timeline work together so users can explore multiple environments as evolving scenes. We considered scientific integrity, clear NASA attribution, usability, and connectivity: the interface distinguishes NASA imagery from simulated motion, and notes that online imagery and map tiles require internet access.
